# A sharp two-tail inequality for a planar concave section density

This is an exact one-dimensional functional lemma for the parallel-section
density of one actual planar convex body. It retains the dependence of
two tails of the SAME density. It does not assert a mixed-depth theorem,
simultaneous realization of different cap directions, or exclusion of
every formal scalar menu.

## 1. Statement and sharp equality

Let f:[0,1]->[0,infinity) be concave, measurable, finite-valued, and have
integral 1. Let 0<x<y<1 and define

    A=integral_x^1 f(t)dt,       B=integral_y^1 f(t)dt.

Then

    (1-y)^2 <= B <= 1-y^2,                             (1)

    A >= (1-x)^2
        +[x(1-x)/(y(1-y))][B-(1-y)^2].                 (2)

For each B in the entire interval (1), equality in (2) is attained.
Set

    lambda=[B-(1-y)^2]/[2y(1-y)] in [0,1].

The equality density is uniquely, up to equality almost everywhere,

    f(t)=2(1-lambda)(1-t)+2lambda t.                    (3)

If f is continuous on [0,1], equality is pointwise affine. For a merely
finite nonnegative concave f, its specified endpoint values may be lower
than its one-sided limits without affecting either tail; this harmless
endpoint freedom is the only qualification to pointwise equality.

Both x and y are strictly interior and distinct. If x=y, the displayed
tail inequality becomes an identity and the equality characterization
above no longer applies. Endpoints x=0 or y=1 likewise require separate
degenerate interpretations and are excluded from the statement.

## 2. Exact positive representation by normalized tents

For p in (0,1), define the normalized tent

    T_p(t)=2t/p                  for 0<=t<=p,
           2(1-t)/(1-p)         for p<=t<=1.

At the endpoint peaks set T_0(t)=2(1-t) and T_1(t)=2t. Every T_p is
nonnegative and concave, has integral 1, and has maximum at most 2.

First suppose f is continuous on the closed interval. Its right
derivative h=f'_+ exists and is finite on (0,1), is nonincreasing and
right-continuous there. Define the positive Stieltjes curvature measure
nu on (0,1) by nu((a,b])=h(a)-h(b), for 0<a<b<1. It may have infinite
total mass near endpoints; all weighted integrals below remain finite.

We prove the needed Green-kernel identity explicitly. On a compact
subinterval [a,b] of (0,1), f is Lipschitz and hence absolutely continuous.
Integrating h(s)=h(a)-nu((a,s]) and applying Tonelli gives

    f(t)=f(a)+(t-a)h(a)-integral_(a,t] (t-p)nu(dp).

Use the same formula at b and subtract the chord from a to b. This gives

    f(t)-[(b-t)f(a)+(t-a)f(b)]/(b-a)
       =integral_(a,b) G_ab(t,p)nu(dp),               (4)

where, for a<t,p<b,

    G_ab(t,p)=[min(t,p)-a][b-max(t,p)]/(b-a).

Extend this kernel by zero outside (a,b). As a decreases to 0 and b
increases to 1, it increases to

    G(t,p)=min(t,p)-tp.

For completeness, if m=min(t,p) and M=max(t,p), differentiating
(m-a)(b-M)/(b-a) gives a nonpositive derivative in a and a nonnegative
derivative in b. New portions of the domain have nonnegative kernel.
Thus monotone convergence in (4), together with endpoint continuity,
proves

    f(t)=f(0)(1-t)+f(1)t+integral_(0,1) G(t,p)nu(dp). (5)

Since G(t,p)=p(1-p)T_p(t)/2, this is an exact positive tent mixture.
Indeed let mu have endpoint masses f(0)/2,f(1)/2, and interior measure

    mu(dp)=[p(1-p)/2]nu(dp).

Integrating (5) in t and using nonnegativity and Tonelli proves

    mu([0,1])=1,          f(t)=integral T_p(t)mu(dp). (6)

Thus the mixture is a probability measure even when nu itself is infinite.
No exchange of conditionally convergent integrals is used.

For general finite nonnegative concave f of integral 1, concavity and
nonnegative endpoint values give f(t)<=2 for every t in (0,1): the two
triangles beneath its graph with common height f(t) have total integral
f(t)/2. A bounded concave function has finite one-sided endpoint limits;
replace its two endpoint values by these limits. This is a continuous
concave representative on [0,1] with the same integral and tails. Apply
the preceding argument to that representative. This proves (6) almost
everywhere in the original generality and explains the equality convention.

There is also a direct approximation justification. Polygonal interpolants
of a continuous concave f along uniform meshes remain nonnegative and
concave and converge uniformly, by uniform continuity of f. After division
by their integrals, they still converge uniformly to f. Their curvature
measure is a finite positive sum of atoms at the interior knots, so (6)
is an ordinary finite positive mixture. All tail functionals converge.
This verifies passage from finite tent calculations without replacing the
two dependent tails by independently chosen scalar extremizers.

## 3. The tent curve is globally concave

Write A_p and B_p for the tails of T_p at x and y. Direct integration gives

    A_p=(1-x)^2/(1-p),  p<=x;
    A_p=1-x^2/p,        p>=x,                         (7)

and the same formulas with y in place of x for B_p. The endpoint
interpretations are continuous. In particular B_p is strictly increasing
in p, from b0=(1-y)^2 to b1=1-y^2. This proves (1) for every mixture.

Regard A_p as a function F(B_p). Its three pieces are

    F(B)=[(1-x)^2/(1-y)^2]B,                          p<=x;
    F(B)=1-x^2-x^2(1-y)^2/[B-(1-y)^2],               x<=p<=y;
    F(B)=1-(x^2/y^2)(1-B),                            y<=p. (8)

The middle derivative and second derivative are

    F'(B)=x^2(1-y)^2/[B-(1-y)^2]^2,
    F''(B)=-2x^2(1-y)^2/[B-(1-y)^2]^3<0.

At p=x the first derivative equals (1-x)^2/(1-y)^2, and at p=y
it equals x^2/y^2. These are precisely the adjacent linear slopes.
Consequently F is continuously differentiable and concave on its entire
closed domain, and strictly concave on its nonempty middle interval.

Its endpoint chord has slope

    [(1-x^2)-(1-x)^2]/[(1-y^2)-(1-y)^2]
       =x(1-x)/[y(1-y)]=c.                           (9)

Concavity puts each point of F above this chord. The inequality is strict
at every p in (0,1). To check strictness including the two linear pieces,
their slopes satisfy

    (1-x)^2/(1-y)^2 > c > x^2/y^2,

both equivalent to y>x after cancellation of positive factors. More
explicitly the gap g(p)=A_p-(1-x)^2-c[B_p-(1-y)^2] is

    [(1-x)(y-x)/y] p/(1-p),                          0<=p<=x;
    [x(y-x)/(1-y)] (1-p)/p,                          y<=p<=1,

and the middle interval is strictly above its positive endpoint gaps
by concavity. Thus g is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at p=0,1,
and is strictly positive at every interior peak.

Integrating the pointwise chord inequality in the probability mixture
(6) proves (2). Equality means integral g(p)mu(dp)=0, which forces mu
to be supported on {0,1}. Equation (6) gives exactly (3). Conversely
every density (3) has tails on the endpoint chord, and its coefficient
lambda yields the specified B. This proves sharpness and every stated
equality assertion.

## 4. A known lower bound on the far tail

Suppose only that B>=delta, where 0<=delta<=1. If delta>1-y^2 no
such density exists. Otherwise the exact best lower bound is

    A >= (1-x)^2
       +[x(1-x)/(y(1-y))][delta-(1-y)^2]_+.          (10)

Here [r]_+=max(r,0). Indeed (1) and B>=delta imply
B>=max(delta,(1-y)^2), and the chord slope is positive. If
delta<=(1-y)^2 the decreasing endpoint cone T_0 attains (10).
If delta>(1-y)^2 the affine density (3) with B=delta attains it.

Equality in (10) is unique almost everywhere: it is T_0 when
delta<=(1-y)^2, and otherwise it is the affine density with B=delta.
There is no unproved assumption that a cone minimizing the early tail
also independently satisfies a prescribed far-tail mass.

## 5. Translation to one actual planar cap

Let D be a full-dimensional planar convex body with a nonconstant affine
height s ranging exactly over [0,H], H>0. Put w=|D|. In coordinates
perpendicular and parallel to its height lines, write sigma(s) for
section length divided by the Euclidean norm of the height's linear
coefficient. Then w=integral_0^H sigma(s)ds by Fubini. The density sigma
is nonnegative and concave: convex combinations of two section intervals
are contained in the intermediate section, so their lengths satisfy
the one-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski inequality directly. Therefore

    f(t)=H sigma(Ht)/w

is a normalized concave density to which the preceding theorem applies.
Every tail is the volume of the corresponding ACTUAL portion of D.

In the canonical three-cap application let

    D=A intersect {v_l.p>=-1},  |D|=w,
    H=h_A(v_l)+1>3,
    |A intersect {v_l.p>=2}|>=delta,  r=delta/w.

For -2<t<1 put x=(1-t)/H and y=3/H. Then 0<x<y<1 and

    |A intersect {v_l.p>=-t}|/w
       >= (1-(1-t)/H)^2
          +[(1-t)(H-1+t)/(3(H-3))]
                        [r-(1-3/H)^2]_+.           (11)

Feasibility additionally requires r<=1-9/H^2, equivalently
H>=3/sqrt(1-r) when r<1. The coefficient in (11) is the exact
ratio x(1-x)/(y(1-y)); the H^2 factors cancel. All quantities refer
to the same actual captured body D, not to different extremal cones.

When equality at a prescribed interior pair holds, D has affine section
length in this direction. Such a planar convex D is a trapezoid, allowing
a triangle if one endpoint length is zero: write each section as an
interval [l(s),u(s)]. Convexity makes l convex and u concave. If u-l is
affine, their nonnegative Jensen deficits sum to zero, so both functions
are affine. Closure supplies the endpoint sections. This is one-direction
rigidity only, and says nothing about simultaneous cap realizability.

The actual affine-density scalar witness and its surviving bulk-capacity
inequalities are recorded independently in Section 7 of
`candidate 921f72bdedb6df67`.
In particular this sharp lemma must not be promoted to closure of that
remaining geometric branch.

## 6. The entire feasible two-tail region

The same proof gives both boundaries of the exact feasible set, if an
upper constraint is also useful. With F from (8) and the chord L from
(2), every concave density satisfies

    b0<=B<=b1,            L(B)<=A<=F(B).             (12)

Indeed each tangent line to the concave differentiable F lies above
its whole graph. Integrating the tangent inequality at the actual
mean B against mu gives A=integral F(B_p)mu(dp)<=F(B).
This proves the upper bound directly without interchanging extrema.

Conversely every pair in (12) is realized. Since p->B_p is continuous
and strictly increasing, choose the unique p with B_p=B. The density
T_p realizes (F(B),B), while the endpoint mixture (3) realizes
(L(B),B). A convex combination of these two densities realizes every
intermediate A, remains nonnegative and concave, and still has mass 1.
Thus (12) describes the full two-tail region, not merely necessary
separate scalar bounds.

For completeness, upper-bound equality has these exact cases. Put
Bx=(1-y)^2/(1-x) and By=1-y. If Bx<B<By, equality requires mu to be
supported at the unique peak p with B_p=B, so f=T_p almost everywhere.
If b0<=B<=Bx, equality holds precisely for mixtures supported on
p in [0,x] with the specified B. If By<=B<=b1, it holds precisely
for mixtures supported on [y,1]. This follows from the tangent contact
set of F: its two linear pieces and its strictly concave middle piece.
At the joins, the tangent contact set is the adjacent entire linear
piece; the descriptions include those endpoints. The lower equality
class remains exactly the affine densities proved in Section 3.
